articles.title: In 1856, a photographer captured a man whose identity was forgotten; after selling in 2025 as an unknown sitter, the portrait was traced to New York's first licensed Black lawyer and sold for $230,400
articles.summary: A photograph that sold for just $882 at a New York auction last year has fetched $230,400 a year later after experts discovered the identity of the man
articles.body: A photograph that sold for just $882 at a New York auction last year has fetched $230,400 a year later after experts discovered the identity of the man pictured in it. The 170-year-old image, which had been listed as a portrait of an unknown man wearing spectacles, was identified as a photograph of George Boyer Vashon, the first licensed African American lawyer in New York State. The discovery also revealed that the photograph had been taken in 1856 by Philip Haas, a 19th-century photographer.The portrait originally offered by Christie's as part of the Maillet Daguerreotype Collection was described as "A well-dressed man with spectacles", and neither the person pictured nor the photographer was named. Despite an estimated value of $1,000 to $1,500, the photograph sold for $882.This year, Sotheby's sold the same portrait for $230,400, more than two and a half times its upper estimate of $90,000 after specialists established who the man was and who had photographed him. The findings gave the image a direct connection to an important figure in American legal and civil rights history.According to Sotheby's, the discovery began when photography specialist Emily Bierman examined the unidentified portrait. When she looked more closely at the object, she found two details that had not been reflected in the Christie's listing: a photographer's signature and an inscription preserved inside the case.Inside the photograph's caseThe first important detail was the marking "P Haas NY", which linked the photograph to Philip Haas. The photographer was active between the 1830s and 1860s. His identification helped establish who had produced the portrait, but it did not immediately explain who was sitting for the photograph.The answer came from the case in which the image had been preserved. An extensive inscription inside it provided the information needed to identify the man as George Boyer Vashon.The object itself was a sixth-plate daguerreotype, an early type of photograph made on a specially prepared metal plate. The image also had hand-applied colouring and gilt detailing. It was kept in a leather case fitted with a push-button closure.The findings also clarified the photograph's date. Christie's had listed it as dating to around 1850, while Sotheby's identified the portrait as having been made in 1856.Who was George Boyer Vashon?The man in the photograph, George Boyer Vashon, was known for his contributions to law, education and civil rights in the United States. He became the first licensed African American attorney in New York State and was also an abolitionist and educator.Sotheby's described him as an influential advocate for civil rights. His work extended beyond the legal profession, making his identification particularly significant for a photograph that had previously been catalogued without a name.How photograph reached the two auctionsBefore its appearance at Christie's, the portrait had passed through private collections. Sotheby's records show that it belonged to Josephine Cobb before being acquired by Lynn and Yann Maillet in the 1980s.The photograph remained associated with the Maillet collection until it was offered at Christie's in June 2025 as Lot 81. Its catalogue entry did not identify Haas or Vashon, so the final selling price was below the auction house's estimate.Following the subsequent identification, Sotheby's included the portrait as Lot 206 in its Fine Books and Manuscripts, Including Americanas sale in New York on June 25, 2026.The auction house placed an estimate of $60,000 to $90,000 on the photograph. Bidding took the final price to $230,400, far exceeding that range.The two sales, held almost exactly a year apart, showed a substantial difference in how the same photograph was presented and valued.You use AI every day. articles.title: Atlanta rapper Shawty Dred indicted in alleged $4 million SNAP fraud, accused of using stolen identities, fake accounts and EBT cards to siphon taxpayer money and fund a lavish lifestyle
articles.summary: Social media personality Mercedes Reshard New, known online as Shawty Dred, has been indicted on federal charges in an alleged fraud scheme involving more
articles.body: Social media personality Mercedes Reshard New, known online as Shawty Dred, has been indicted on federal charges in an alleged fraud scheme involving more than $4 million in US food assistance benefits. Prosecutors allege that the 39-year-old Atlanta resident used stolen identities to create hundreds of fraudulent accounts and fund a lavish lifestyle showcased on social media.According to the US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Georgia, a federal grand jury indicted New on October 7, 2026. He faces 46 counts of mail fraud, 15 counts of aggravated identity theft, and one count each of SNAP fraud and illegal transactions involving access devices. He was arrested on October 13 and remains in the custody of the US Marshals Service pending further proceedings.Shawty Dred allegedly controlled more than 350 fraudulent SNAP accountsAccording to the indictment, the alleged scheme ran from January 2020 to July 2026. Prosecutors claim New controlled more than 350 fraudulent Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) accounts created using stolen identities.Investigators allege that he arranged for electronic benefit transfer (EBT) debit cards to be mailed to multiple addresses across the Atlanta metropolitan area. He also allegedly applied for his company, Shawty Dred LLC, to become an authorised SNAP retailer.Between April 2024 and November 2025, New allegedly used fraudulently obtained EBT cards and a point-of-sale device associated with his company to obtain more than $660,000 in SNAP benefits.In November 2025, the US Department of Agriculture revoked his store’s authorisation. Around two weeks later, local police allegedly arrested New at a store in the Atlanta area for selling SNAP benefits. Officers reportedly seized 14 EBT cards issued to other individuals.Prosecutors further allege that, after the cards were seized, New arranged for replacement cards to be sent to his store and other addresses around Atlanta.Prosecutors allege $4.6 million in benefits were transferredThe indictment alleges that New deceived Georgia’s Division of Family and Children Services into transferring approximately $4.6 million in SNAP benefits to fraudulently established beneficiary accounts. EBT cards were then allegedly used to siphon approximately $4 million from those accounts.SNAP is a federal programme administered by the US Department of Agriculture that provides monthly food assistance to eligible low-income households. In Georgia, the programme is administered by the Department of Human Services’ Division of Family and Children Services. Beneficiaries use EBT cards to purchase eligible food items, and selling or trading SNAP benefits is prohibited.US Attorney Theodore S. Hertzberg alleged that the money involved was intended to help struggling families afford food.“My office is fully committed to rooting out abuses of the SNAP program and holding accountable criminal con artists and scammers,” Hertzberg said in a statement, referring to the alleged misuse of taxpayer money intended to feed vulnerable Americans.FBI Atlanta Special Agent in Charge Marlo Graham also alleged that the money was used to finance a luxurious lifestyle rather than support families in need.Shawty Dred’s luxury lifestyle on Instagram and TikTokNew has more than two million followers on his Instagram account, richlifeshawtydred. According to the US Attorney’s Office, his social media posts have featured private jet travel, luxury Rolls-Royce and Maybach vehicles, and large stacks of cash.USDA Inspector General John Walk said New allegedly flaunted his lifestyle online while exploiting food assistance benefits in Georgia. Federal authorities said the case was investigated by the USDA Office of Inspector General and the FBI, with assistance from the Georgia Department of Human Services’ Office of Inspector General.Assistant US Attorney Tracia M. King is prosecuting the case.Shawty Dred is presumed innocentThe indictment contains allegations, not findings of guilt. New is presumed innocent unless and until prosecutors prove the charges against him beyond a reasonable doubt in court.The case comes as the US Department of Justice continues its efforts to investigate and prosecute alleged fraud involving federal benefit programmes. The department announced the creation of its National Fraud Enforcement Division on April 7, 2026, as part of a broader government initiative targeting fraud, waste and abuse.The proceedings against New are ongoing.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2018, inventor Colin Furze began a tunnel for the joy of making; three years later, it linked his home and workshop, with a bunker next, beneath his garden
articles.summary: Discover how British inventor Colin Furze connected his home, workshop, and bunker with an extraordinary DIY underground tunnel project, gaining millions of YouTube followers along the way.
articles.body: British YouTube personality Colin Furze started digging a tunnel in November 2018 beneath his garden in Stamford, Lincolnshire. The goal behind the project was to connect his house to his workshop and, eventually, an underground bunker. After three years of construction, the passage developed into a full-fledged project with steel and concrete supports, lighting, ventilation and a track system for removing excavated soil. The work went ahead without any planning permission until Furze submitted an application to South Kesteven District Council in April 2022. By the time the project received a stamp of approval, much of the digging had already been finished. The approval followed serious concerns regarding the potential effects on health, safety and ground stability.A secret excavation developed into an engineered underground passageFurze’s project germinated with a practical idea which would allow him to reach his bunker without having to go outside through the garden path. He initially worked with a shovel, filling a single bucket at a time, and dug the tunnel approximately 1.2 metres (4 feet) below ground level, connecting his kitchen pantry with his shedAlthough the excavation was supposed to be kept from the neighbours, it gradually developed into a more elaborate construction, requiring more equipment and structural material to secure the passage. The tunnel was reinforced with steel and concrete, and its interior was fitted with lighting and ventilation shafts. In December 2022, ITV News Anglia reported that in order to minimise the noise generated during construction, Furze invented specialised mining equipment, which included a hydraulic jackhammer. Owing to these preventive measures, he was able to continue his work underground and keep his activities unnoticed on the street.The project also gained a digital footprint when it was released as a YouTube series titled Digging a Secret Tunnel. Although Furze anticipated that the construction would only provide content for a few videos, it unfolded into a series of nine instalments by June 2022. His audience followed the development from the early excavation through the installation of the tunnel's supporting structures and equipment.According to the BBC’s report published on 19 June 2022, Furze had gained 12 million YouTube followers at the time. The coverage also recorded his explanation for undertaking the project: he thought it would be cool. Before the tunnel, Furze had also worked on other unusual engineering projects, including experimental vehicles and other large-scale builds. Moreover, the underground bunker had also received recognition outside his YouTube channel and won the 2020 Cuprinol Shed of the Year competition, as reported by the Evening Standard.Planning approval came with conditions on further constructionThe tunnel’s development eventually came to the attention of South Kesteven District Council after the plans circulated widely on Facebook. Consequently, the site was visited by a planning inspector, and the application was considered regardless. The approval was met with objections from the parish council, which raised concerns relating to health and safety and the possibility of subsidence. Ultimately, on 10 June 2022, the council granted retrospective planning permission, but it came with a condition that required the ground and the structural integrity of the construction to be investigated before further work proceeded.However, the decision didn’t automatically authorise every part of Furze’s proposed underground connection. He had already set his sights on a new stage which would involve a digger to extend the passage between the shed and the bunker. This would cover approximately 15 metres (49 feet) and would require additional planning permission to go through. The distinction mattered because the bunker and the tunnel had separate planning histories. Homebuilding & Renovating reported that permission for the bunker had been granted in 2014, while the tunnel was built without approval and subsequently received retrospective consent.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bulldozers tear down home as Israel cracks down in the West Bank
articles.summary: Bulldozers tore down Palestinian businessman Riyad Mureish’s home in Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday, as Israeli officials launched a fresh crackdown on residents there.
articles.body: Bulldozers tore down Palestinian businessman Riyad Mureish’s home in Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday, as Israeli officials launched a fresh crackdown on residents there. Mureish, 49, who put his life savings into the house, told NBC News that Israeli soldiers gave his family just minutes to collect their valuables and identity documents before ordering them out. He said the house had been subject to a long-running dispute with Israeli authorities, who retain significant power over construction permits in the area. A court decree was in place that should have prevented any demolition, Mureish added, but the soldiers were unswayed by his pleas. “They demolished and took me out by force,” he said. Now sheltering in a small room at a neighbor’s house with his wife and children, Mureish says he is still struggling to comprehend what has happened. He said: “No house, no land, no money, what can I do?” Videos captured the moment that bulldozers began to rip through the property. The scenes unfolded the same day that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stood in another part of Hebron, wearing a military-style vest, and vowed to intensify operations across the occupied West Bank. After a shooting attack that left two Israeli soldiers and two gunmen dead, Netanyahu said the military would enter neighborhoods from which attackers had emerged, evacuate residents and go “house to house” to tackle any threat. “We are going to destroy terrorist infrastructure, and we are going to build the infrastructure for settlement,” he told cameras, speaking days before Israel’s pivotal Oct. 27 election that will decide whether he stays in power. Israeli forces have since “sealed off all the entrances” to the city, “making it impossible for anyone to enter or leave,” according to Yousef al-Jabari, the Palestinian mayor of Hebron. He told NBC News a key mosque had been forced to close and residents in some areas were being removed from their homes, adding that soldiers have “effectively besieged an entire densely populated area and are demanding that its residents leave.” Hebron is the largest city in the West Bank, home to approximately 320,000 people. Israeli human rights organization B’Tselem said approximately 240 Palestinian families were forced from their homes in the Jildah and ‘Ein Deir Bahah neighborhoods of Hebron on Friday and Saturday. “Soldiers have taken over numerous homes and remain inside them, raising Israeli flags over several buildings. Arrests and interrogations are also continuing,” the group said in a statement. Tensions have soared in the West Bank in the weeks before the Israeli election, with a spate of settler violence and military activity centered on the start of the olive harvesting season. Palestinians, activists and American journalists have been among those attacked and detained. Al-Jabari called the latest lockdown a “form of collective punishment” and suggested Netanyahu’s intervention was motivated by politics. “With the Israeli elections only days away, Netanyahu is seeking to secure as many votes as possible by appeasing the settlers,” he said. Netanyahu has long faced pressure from his far-right allies to embrace harder stances in the West Bank. In his comments Friday, he praised settlers as “heroic,” saying they were “an example to the people of Israel and to the state of Israel.” The leader, facing a tough re-election battle, has focused much of his campaign ahead of Tuesday’s vote on security. His government has repeatedly warned of potential attacks by the country’s “enemies” in the lead-up to the election, without providing evidence. In the wake of Friday’s attack, he said that he had “warned several weeks ago about our enemies’ attempts to harm us, our civilians and our soldiers ahead of the elections. That is what they tried to here.” U.N. spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric said at a press briefing Friday that “closures severely restrict Palestinians’ freedom of movement, access to basic services and livelihoods.” Mayy El Sheikh, a spokesperson for the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights in the Occupied Palestinian Territory, said in a statement Friday that the lockdown was “yet another episode in a never-ending stream of suffocating measures making life more and more unbearable for Palestinians.” “It follows a pattern of collective punishment whenever Palestinians commit acts of violence against Israeli settlers or soldiers,” she said. H.A. Hellyer, a senior associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute in London, told NBC News that Netanyahu could be showing a “strong arm” ahead of the elections by locking down the West Bank, but he said the link was not clear, noting that the main candidates in the election were broadly aligned. Even if Netanyahu loses, he said, “I don’t expect there to be change on the West Bank.” Israeli officials did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: In 1991, inspired by Dutch castles, Casper Noz rejected his house plans and began a family home in Snelling, California; its two towers now host weddings
articles.summary: Discover Castle Noz, a stunning medieval-style castle built by Dutch contractor Casper Noz in California. With its two towers and enchanting design, it now serves as a unique venue for weddings and events.
articles.body: Dutch-born contractor Casper Noz began building a medieval-style castle in 1991, and more than three decades later, Castle Noz, near Snelling, has two completed four-storey towers at its entrance, and the property hosts weddings and other private events while construction continues.Noz’s own history of the property says that he and his wife, Diane, bought the land for a family home. He had initially worked on high-rise buildings in San Francisco and later established himself as a contractor in the Central Valley. The castle’s construction began in 1991, and the couple started hosting events in the late 1990s, according to the venue’s website.Dutch architecture shaped the designNoz grew up in the Netherlands and wanted to recreate the look of the castles that he remembered from home. The Merced County Times said that he drew up seven designs before settling on a medieval style based on Dutch castles from roughly AD 600 to 1400. He bought the land with Diane in 1987 and planted more than 500 oak trees on the property.Noz has done much of the work himself, such as laying bricks, making doors, and crafting metal hinges, latches, and handles. The finished plan calls for about 12,000 square feet of castle space, with the entrance towers forming the completed front section and a larger rear structure still under construction.The Merced County Times described the two towers as four levels tall, with wooden spiral staircases that lead to lookout terraces, while the interiors combine medieval-style details with practical facilities, including rooms for guests and bathrooms. Noz has also planned a moat and drawbridges for the expanded complex.Noz has relied on his own masonry and metalworking skills to produce many of the details, from the doors and staircases to the iron fittings, with the work taking place alongside his contracting career, and the castle expanding as time and resources have allowed. The Merced County Times documented the project’s gradual progress and Noz’s plans for additional towers, a moat and drawbridges.A family project that became an event venueNoz worked on the castle around his contracting jobs, and often used weekends to build the structure brick by brick. A 2008 report by The New York Times, republished by SFGATE, described him mixing mortar, making wooden doors and staircases, and forging iron hardware by hand, with an estimate of about 500 hours a year spent on the project. Noz wanted a grand entrance, and memories of the castles in his Dutch hometown of ’s-Hertogenbosch pushed him toward a different design. The castle was intended as a future retirement home for Noz and Diane, rather than a building that was designed from the outset for public events.The family eventually began welcoming other people to the property after friends asked whether they could hold a wedding there. Castle Noz’s official history places the start of public events in the late 1990s, and now advertises weddings alongside reunions, birthday parties, school events and other gatherings. The completed entrance section provides the facilities that were used for events while the rest of the castle remains unfinished.The castle is still a work in progress, and Noz’s original plan was to move into it with Diane once construction was complete, but the larger rear section and proposed additions have taken years to build. For now, the two towers at the entrance are the most visible finished part of a project that began with a plan for an ordinary family house.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Ina Garten’s secret to creamy scrambled eggs is an unexpected Italian staple
articles.summary: Ina Garten's ricotta scrambled eggs rival Gordon Ramsay's crème fraîche method, creating a custardy texture with chives, Parmesan and red pepper flakes.
articles.body: Gordon Ramsay and Bobby Flay swear by adding a bit of crème fraîche to their scrambled eggs. Alton Brown's unconventional approach calls for mayonnaise and extra egg yolks. Ina Garten, however, puts her own Italian-inspired spin on the breakfast favorite. The key to perfect scrambled eggs is ricotta cheese, the "Barefoot Contessa" star recently told the Wall Street Journal. CELEBRITY CHEF LEAVES ONE ICONIC INGREDIENT OUT OF HER FRENCH COOKING AND DINERS CAN'T TELL "How you cook the eggs makes such a difference, too," Garten said. "If you cook them at a very low heat and add ricotta to give it creaminess and a little texture, it’s just a whole other thing." She added, "It’s like a custard rather than scrambled eggs." YOU'RE PROBABLY COOKING RICE WRONG, AND CHEFS REVEAL THE SIMPLE MISTAKE TO AVOID Garten also recommends adding any herbs that you have on hand. "I put chives in it," she said. Her method has one thing in common with Ramsay’s approach: Both chefs rely on gentle cooking to keep the eggs soft. Ramsay adds the crème fraîche cold at the end to stop the cooking and bring richness to the dish. Garten instead folds ricotta into the eggs as they cook, leaving some small curds visible, according to the Journal. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER Her recipe, adapted from her cookbook "Simply Ina," serves four and calls for eggs, milk, butter, olive oil and ricotta. She heats the butter and olive oil over medium-low and lets the eggs, which are whisked with milk, salt and pepper, set briefly at the edges before stirring constantly until they’re soft and custardy. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Garten suggests serving the eggs on buttered toast, with chives, Parmesan and red pepper flakes. She also shared other simple tips to elevate everyday dishes beyond breakfast. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ For last-minute appetizers, she makes an "emergency blue-cheese dip" with blue cheese and mayonnaise, then serves it with whatever vegetables she has in the fridge. Potato chips, olives, salami and cucumber slices also make her list of easy, go-to snacks. For dessert, Garten told the Journal, she’ll buy a cheesecake from a good bakery and make a quick raspberry sauce to serve with it. "Nobody will ever know," she said. "You’re relaxed. The dessert is delicious. Everybody has a good time." articles.body: Sunday night is Kojagari Purnima, and for Taurus it brings welcome support to a struggling ruler. Venus, lord of your sign, has spent days buried in the Sun’s glare in Libra, your sixth, and is still retrograde. Having just passed the Sun, it now begins its slow climb back towards visibility. Goddess Lakshmi, worshipped tonight, shares Venus’s qualities of abundance and grace, so her puja strengthens your planet. The full Moon itself falls in Aries, your twelfth, and Shani stays retrograde in your eleventh.Lakshmi and VenusIn jyotish, Venus governs comfort and wealth, gifts closely associated with Lakshmi. articles.title: A New York couple lost two baby raccoons after failing to find them help; they later built a wildlife rescue centre and have since helped more than 800 raccoons
articles.summary: When Paul and Sarah Bookbinder tried to save two abandoned baby raccoons in 2017, they struggled to find a wildlife rehabilitator who could take them in.
articles.body: When Paul and Sarah Bookbinder tried to save two abandoned baby raccoons in 2017, they struggled to find a wildlife rehabilitator who could take them in. The kits, named Stanley and Laurel, died within days, leaving the couple determined to help other animals in similar circumstances. In 2018, they established the Charles N. Gordon Wildlife Rehabilitation Center on a 53-acre property in Earlville, central New York. Sarah, a licensed wildlife rehabilitator, and Paul, a board-certified veterinary surgeon, have since rehabilitated more than 800 injured and orphaned raccoons, releasing those capable of surviving independently. Their work also includes providing long-term care for animals whose injuries or disabilities prevent them from returning to the wild.How the loss of two raccoons inspired the centreThe couple's wildlife rescue journey began when a neighbour brought them two abandoned raccoon kits. Although Paul had extensive veterinary experience, his clinical work focused on cats and dogs, and the couple lacked the specialist knowledge and facilities needed to care for the young raccoons.They contacted potential rehabilitators but could not find one able to take the animals. Stanley and Laurel died a few days later. The experience exposed a gap in access to specialist wildlife care and prompted the Bookbinders to establish a dedicated rehabilitation facility.The centre was named after Paul's late uncle, Charles N. Gordon. An inheritance from his uncle helped the couple make the down payment on the property where the centre was established.A 53-acre property dedicated to wildlife rehabilitationLocated in Earlville, the centre occupies 53 acres of wooded wetlands adjoining protected state forest. The property provides space for the rehabilitation operation, including enclosures where raccoons can recover and develop the behaviours they need to survive outside captivity.The centre was founded in 2018 and focuses on orphaned and injured raccoons. It also supports other wildlife rehabilitators by sharing veterinary expertise and practical guidance on animal care.Paul and Sarah contribute their time and personal resources to the operation. Sarah oversees animal care, volunteers, interns and the centre's daily administration, while Paul handles medical procedures requiring veterinary expertise.Bottle-feeding hundreds of baby raccoons each springSpring is the centre's busiest period, when young raccoons arrive after being orphaned, injured or separated from their mothers. Some are brought in by members of the public, while others come through veterinarians, wildlife officials and other rehabilitation contacts.The youngest kits require frequent feeding with species-appropriate formula. Depending on their age and needs, they may need to be fed between two and eight times a day. Sarah has described the scale of the work during peak season, when she has prepared more than 200 bottles in a day.As the animals grow, the centre gradually moves them towards eating solid food and developing the skills needed for life in the wild.Teaching raccoons to forage and avoid peopleRehabilitation involves more than nursing an animal back to health. Raccoons must learn to find food, climb, explore and avoid humans before they can be released safely.At around three months old, kits are moved into enclosures where food such as nuts, eggs, worms and crickets is hidden in the soil to encourage natural foraging. Structures such as ladders, hammocks and tyre swings allow them to practise climbing and moving through their surroundings.The Bookbinders limit unnecessary human interaction to reduce the risk of the animals becoming habituated to people. Signs of independence, including hiding from humans and attempting to escape, help indicate whether a raccoon is ready for release. Releases generally take place in late summer or early autumn, once the animals can fend for themselves.More than 800 raccoons have been rehabilitatedSince the centre opened, the Bookbinders estimate that they have rehabilitated more than 800 raccoons. The animals arrive with a range of problems, including injuries, illness and the loss of their mothers. Their outcomes vary according to the severity of their conditions and their ability to recover.In one case reported by The Washington Post, a raccoon that struggled to use its forelegs began climbing after arriving at the centre. The animal gradually regained strength and was eventually released after about eight months.Not every raccoon can return to the wild. The centre continues to care for roughly two dozen animals whose disabilities or injuries make independent survival unlikely. These include Peanut, who has a vestibular condition affecting his ability to climb down, and Tribble, who was born with legs too short for climbing.Veterinary care and equipment help treat injured animalsThe centre has also worked to improve the medical care available to raccoons. Transporting severely injured animals to other facilities can be stressful, and access to diagnostic equipment is important when assessing fractures and other injuries.In 2022, the centre acquired a single-wide trailer to serve as an in-house wildlife medical facility. A $10,000 grant from the Dr Robert J. Vitkus Fund helped it purchase an X-ray machine.The equipment allows the team to assess injuries on-site and has also been used to assist animals being treated by other wildlife rehabilitators. Paul's surgical expertise complements Sarah's rehabilitation work, allowing the centre to provide specialist care that can be difficult to access elsewhere.Sharing their expertise with other wildlife rehabilitatorsThe Bookbinders' work extends beyond the animals at their own facility. They co-authored Gordon Wildlife Raccoon Rehabilitation Protocols, a reference of more than 200 pages covering feeding, housing, medical care and rehabilitation practices.The guide has been used by wildlife professionals across numerous US states and other countries. The centre also offers educational outreach, workshops and training to help other rehabilitators improve their care practices.By sharing their experience, the couple aim to strengthen wildlife rehabilitation beyond their own property, particularly for raccoons that require specialist attention.Remembering the animals they could not saveThe emotional toll of wildlife rehabilitation remains part of the couple's work. Animals sometimes arrive with injuries too severe to treat, and the Bookbinders must make difficult decisions when recovery is not possible.To remember the raccoons that have passed through their care, they engrave the animals' names on rocks placed in a garden among irises and lilacs. The memorial honours both animals that were successfully released and those that died despite their efforts.The couple's work has grown from the loss of two orphaned kits into a specialist rehabilitation operation focused on helping raccoons recover, regain independence and return to the wild whenever possible.You use AI every day. articles.title: Beverly Hills school board candidate under fire over messages mocking trustee's visit to Jewish holy site
articles.summary: Screenshots appeared to show school board candidate Kim Lifschitz mocking a Jewish trustee Russell Stuart's kippah and Western Wall visit, sparking antisemitism claims in Beverly Hills.
articles.body: Beverly Hills school board candidate Kim Lifschitz faced accusations of antisemitism this week after screenshots surfaced appearing to mock a trustee's visit to Jerusalem's Western Wall, while a separate controversy involving her husband's comments featured on a livestream by Twitch streamer Hasan Piker resurfaced. The screenshots show messages labeled with Lifschitz's name responding to a Beverly Hills Standard article documenting Beverly Hills Unified School District Board of Education member Russell Stuart's New Year's Day visit to the Western Wall, one of Judaism's holiest sites. One message attributed to Lifschitz appeared to ridicule his kippah, a traditional Jewish head covering. "Maybe he can bust out the kippah from his dress up trunk," the message said. Another message attributed to Lifschitz appeared later in the conversation, continuing the joke about Stuart's religious head covering, saying, "He probably used it to store his complimentary in-flight nuts." RIHANNA'S BEVERLY HILLS HOME TARGETED IN BRAZEN DAYLIGHT SHOOTING Stuart, whose family is Jewish, condemned the messages in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying political disagreements do not justify ridiculing religious practices. "I found them deeply offensive," he said. "My visit to the Western Wall was personal and meaningful to me. Seeing a kippah described as something from a 'dress up trunk' turns Jewish religious observance into a costume and a punchline." "Anyone is welcome to challenge my votes, my positions or my work on the school board. Mocking my religious observance crosses a very different line," he continued. Lifschitz pushed back against the allegations in a statement to Fox News Digital, acknowledging that the nearly year-old messages came from a private group chat while arguing that her criticism concerned what she described as Stuart's use of Jewish religious symbols to gain political support. "I said nothing antisemitic at all. In fact, I criticized Russell Stuart for disrespecting Jewish culture and observance," she said. "He was treating a kippah like a costume used in a performance, and he afforded it the same amount of respect one would give a container for airplane snacks." "I didn’t 'attack' Russell Stuart for wearing a kippah or visiting the Western Wall," Lifschitz continued. "I expressed disgust that he turned those things into internet content." EXCLUSIVE: INSIDE LA'S HOMELESS HELLSCAPE — UNLIKELY CRITICS BLAST DEMS AS GOP HOPEFUL TOURS SKIR ROW California GOP Jewish Engagement Chair and attorney Elizabeth Barcohana, who has publicly criticized Lifschitz's candidacy, also condemned the school board hopeful, accusing her of being "prejudiced, rude, and unserious about education or the well-being of children." Lifschitz, who identified herself as Jewish, also pointed to her personal experiences with antisemitism when explaining why she questioned Stuart's intentions. "As a Jewish woman who has experienced plenty of antisemitism in her lifetime and who has a son who cannot protect himself from it, it's hardly surprising that I assumed the worst about his intentions, given the evidence available to me," Lifschitz said. A newly circulated screenshot shows a group-chat message labeled with Lifschitz's name appearing to ridicule BHUSD Board Vice President Sigalie Sabag for discussing Holocaust survivors. According to the Beverly Hills Standard, the remark concerned Sabag's discussion of survivors who had spoken with district students. "Love that Sigalie is talking about holocaust survivors like she collected the most Pokémon," the message said. Stuart characterized the comments concerning his religious observance as antisemitic and called on Lifschitz to address them directly. "I consider the remarks attributed to her antisemitic because they ridicule Jewish religious observance and an identifiable symbol of Jewish faith. I cannot speak to what was in her heart, but I can speak to the words," Stuart said. HASAN PIKER POINTS THE FINGER AT AIPAC AS DEMOCRATS SPEAK OUT AGAINST HIM The controversy comes as Lifschitz competes for one of two seats on the BHUSD Board of Education in the Nov. 3 election. During an October interview with the Beverly Press, she emphasized combating discrimination and modeling appropriate behavior for students. "You have to be a role model," she said. "You have to model the conduct that we are expecting from our children." The allegations follow previous scrutiny involving Lifschitz's husband, Daniel Lifschitz, who wrote on Instagram that a clip of him had been featured on far-left streamer Hasan Piker's livestream after publicly criticizing the district's antisemitism resolution, according to a screenshot posted by Barcohana on X. "I just wanted to make some MAGA folks on the school board feel bad and now I'm on [Hasan Piker's] livestream..." Daniel Lifschitz said in an Instagram post. During a September 2025 livestream, Piker replayed a Fox 11 Los Angeles report by Chelsea Edwards concerning the district's decision to reverse a proposal to display Israeli flags during Jewish American Heritage Month. The footage featured Daniel Lifschitz criticizing the original resolution. Piker praised Lifschitz's comments and compared displaying Israeli flags to displaying Nazi flags during a hypothetical German-American heritage commemoration. Kim Lifschitz previously disputed claims that her husband appeared as an invited guest on Piker's program, explaining that the streamer had independently replayed television footage featuring his public remarks. She also defended the private nature of the group-chat conversation, accusing Stuart and his supporters of seeking out critical remarks and using them to portray her negatively. "Adults are allowed to dislike each other and talk about it amongst themselves in private chats," she said. "Seeking out the opinions of those you know dislike you, and then painting them as monsters when you 'catch' them doing what you expected them to do, is the equivalent of putting a stick through the wheel of your own bicycle." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Barcohana criticized the district's previous leadership and teachers' union, arguing that Beverly Hills parents had pushed for greater accountability over school spending and education policy. "Parents in Beverly Hills worked very hard to take control of their children’s education back from the teachers’ union and other special interests, who allowed taxpayer money to be squandered without proper oversight," Barcohana told Fox News Digital. "Once that happened, incompetent and unpopular school principals, teachers, and the superintendent were fired and replaced; student test scores and academic achievement improved, budgets got under control and teacher pay increased to record highs, and enrollment increased," she said.

articles.title: Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden
articles.summary: Houthi missiles reportedly struck a number of targets in Yemen, including Aden’s airport and a coastguard base.
articles.body:
Houthi fighters have launched a series of attacks on targets in Saudi Arabia and the seat of Yemen’s internationally recognised government in Aden.

In a Facebook post on Saturday, the Yemeni government’s Transport Ministry denounced what it described as the Houthis’ targeting of Aden International Airport with two ballistic missiles, calling it the “fourth such attack this month”.

The airport attacks pose “a threat to the safety of civil aviation” and have “humanitarian and economic repercussions for citizens” who rely on it, the ministry warned.

Yemeni authorities said that the coastguard headquarters and a second building were also hit.

The Houthis claimed attacks on the al-Nasr camp and Aden’s naval military base.

Yemen’s army said a Houthi missile killed three people when it malfunctioned and fell on a family home in Houthi-held Sanaa on Friday. The army said it was one of a number of missile malfunctions seen in recent weeks by the Iran-backed group.

Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV said on Saturday that Saudi coalition air strikes killed several civilians in Sanaa and in the port city of Hodeidah. The claim could not be verified and Riyadh has not commented on the alleged raids.

Also on Saturday, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said on X that the Houthis had launched two ballistic missiles towards Mecca and Medina, warning of “the fall of shrapnel” following their interception.

Images shared on X by the Saudi Press Agency appeared to show a large, blackened missile-shaped object that had landed somewhere in Saudi Arabia.

Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, Secretary-General of the Gulf Cooperation Council, described the Houthi attacks as “heinous”, which embody “a blatant disregard for the lives and security of civilians” in a statement shared on Saturday.

The Houthis said the claim that they targeted the two cities – the holiest in Islam – was a “huge lie”. They said their targets were three Saudi airports, oil infrastructure, and an airbase.

The Houthis have persistently targeted Saudi energy infrastructure and airports across the country with long-range strikes since a fragile ceasefire agreed in 2022 fell apart in July.

Intense fighting is continuing on Yemen’s front lines as the Houthis battle forces of the internationally recognised government for control of key areas.

On Saturday, Yemeni army spokesman Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said that government forces had carried out more than 700 “targeting operations” over the last 24 hours across Yemen, “neutralising” 300 Houthi fighters and disabling military vehicles.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify those figures.

Operations targeted field command centres, Houthi gatherings, weapons depots, and supply lines in Taiz, where intense clashes have been ongoing for days, the spokesman added.

articles.title: Indian models make the hometown vs runway trend go viral on social media
articles.summary: Indian models are going viral on social media with the hometown vs runway trend, showcasing their journeys from humble beginnings to the glamour of the fashion world. This trend celebrates roots and challenges societal perceptions of modeling as a privilege.
articles.body: From going about your mundane daily life in your hometown to walking the runway, Indian models are taking a trip down memory lane, showing the world what life looked like before strutting down the fashion runway.What is the trendForget the usual success-story montage. The hometown vs runway trend gives the before-and-after format a fun, sassy twist, juxtaposing the everyday mundanity of life back home with the glamour of the runway. One moment, you’re watching a model draw water from a well, walk through farm fields, carry buckets along narrow village paths, plough the land or tend to their buffaloes; the next, they’re strutting down the runway.Indian models have been taking to Instagram to share these transformations, set to quirky soundtracks that make the contrast all the more entertaining.Savio Fedrick (24), model, actor and producer, who believes he was among the first to start the trend, says, "The idea behind this reel was actually very random. I’ve always loved before-and-after transformations, and I have been experimenting with different reels on Instagram Trials."After multiple experiments, Savio says, "I noticed similar reels performing well with a different audio, and I thought, why not give it another shot? This time, instead of just showing my journey from college to the runway, I wanted to show something more personal—where I come from and where life has taken me. I used one of my favourite Tamil songs from back home, and slowly, the reels started picking up." Savio's reel has now got over 20 million views.Why it's resonatingBeyond the fun transitions and runway glamour, the trend is making a larger point. These models are celebrating their roots while showing that where you come from need not determine how far you can go. Their reels challenge the perception that modelling is a career reserved for the privileged or those from big cities.Interestingly, the trend comes at a time when modelling agencies, which traditionally scouted talent through beauty pageants and in metropolitan cities, are increasingly also looking to smaller towns and rural areas for fresh faces.Take Rituraj Singh Nabiyal (22), an engineering student at IIT Kanpur who is pursuing modelling alongside his studies. Hailing from Nabi, a remote village in Uttarakhand, he has modelled for renowned names in the fashion industry. He says, "Through the reel, I wanted to share my journey and tell those from small towns and rural villages that your background doesn’t define your potential. You can come from a village where farming is the primary occupation and still dream of walking the runway. You don’t have to move to a big city to start believing in yourself."For Savio, too, the reel is as much about reconnecting with his roots as it is about looking back at his journey. "I come from a simple, average Indian family, and I’ve always been a village boy at heart. So, when I look at myself walking on runways today, it’s a very emotional feeling. For me, this reel is not just a before-and-after transformation, but a little reminder of where I started, how far I’ve come, and how much more there is to experience."Some models are giving the trend their own spin. articles.title: Mona Lisa may have had alopecia, dermatologist claims; study explains why her eyebrows and eyelashes are missing
articles.summary: Mona Lisa alopecia is the diagnosis proposed in a new medical study of Leonardo da Vinci's most famous portrait, suggesting the sitter's missing eyebrows
articles.body: Mona Lisa alopecia is the diagnosis proposed in a new medical study of Leonardo da Vinci's most famous portrait, suggesting the sitter's missing eyebrows and eyelashes were caused by alopecia areata universalis, an autoimmune condition that removes hair from the entire body. The study ‘Alopecia areata universalis in Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa: A systematic retrospective iconodiagnosis’ uses retrospective iconodiagnosis, the practice of identifying disease from artworks, and deliberately examines the painted surface rather than the woman herself. Its conclusion is striking, what has often been put down to Renaissance fashion may instead be a careful, accurate and dignified record of illness, painted by an artist famous for observing the human body closely.Why does the Mona Lisa have no eyebrows? A new alopecia diagnosis explains the missing hairThe portrait has long invited medical guesses. Her pale complexion and thinning hair previously prompted claims of thyroid problems, and a scarring hair loss called frontal fibrosing alopecia was suggested more recently. According to The Telegraph, Dr Luigi Laino of the Institute of Dermatology and Trichology in Rome says her missing eyebrows and eyelashes, along with a receding hairline, point instead to the early stages of alopecia. Writing in Clinics in Dermatology, he asks that the painting be recognised for what it has always shown, "a young woman with alopecia areata". His paper also states how its own thesis could be disproved.Four clues hidden in the painting: no eyebrows, no eyelashes, no hairline blend and unscarred skinThe eyebrows are missing completely, on both sides and in a perfectly matching way. They are not thinned or plucked into a fine line. The eyelashes are absent along the whole edge of every eyelid, yet those edges are finely painted, with no sign of damage or smudging. The hairline has no soft transition, a natural one fades through fine, downy hairs, but here it stops abruptly. Finally, the skin around the eyes and across the forehead is smooth and unscarred.Why Renaissance fashion, syphilis, leprosy and other theories fail to explain the missing hairFashion in fifteenth-century Florence favoured a high, bare forehead and slim eyebrows, so it could explain two of the four clues. It cannot explain the eyelashes, which women of the time wanted long and dark, and no tool existed to remove them so close to the eye. Secondary syphilis, lepromatous leprosy (a severe form of leprosy), telogen effluvium (shedding after stress or illness), trichotillomania (compulsive hair pulling) and frontal fibrosing alopecia each fail on at least one key sign. Only alopecia areata universalis fits all four.Nor did Leonardo simply skip the details. He painted eyebrows in earlier portraits, including individually stroked hairs in the Lady with an Ermine. A cleaning accident is also ruled out, because the paint layers around the eyes are thin and intact and a workshop copy in the Prado agrees with the original.The lone hair above the eye: How one tiny strand supports the alopecia areata diagnosisMultispectral imaging, which photographs a painting across 13 bands of light, found one tiny hair above the eye. It had been read as the trace of a painted eyebrow that vanished over time. The study sees a single surviving real hair instead. In alopecia areata the immune system switches hair follicles off rather than destroying them, so a few can keep growing while the rest stay dormant. The paper backs this with a clinical photograph of an eight-year-old patient showing exactly the same feature.If she had alopecia, why does the Mona Lisa have a full head of hair? The Florentine answerThe answer, according to the study, lies in Florentine culture. Fifteenth-century Italy had a thriving trade in real human hair, used to make the capigliara, a structured hairpiece. A married woman also covered her head as a sign of her marital status, so a full, dark, ordered head of hair is not evidence against the diagnosis.A young wife under stress, and why her age fits early alopecia areataAccording to the Italian Art Society, Lisa Gherardini was an Italian woman widely known as the ‘sitter’, she was born in Florence on 15 June 1479, the first of seven children of a noble but modestly wealthy family. She married the widowed silk merchant Francesco del Giocondo on 5 March 1495, aged 15, and had her first child in 1496. The Telegraph reports that Dr Laino also pointed to the loss of two children and the threat of plague, and said stress and hormonal changes can bring on alopecia. The study adds that the condition brings stigma, anxiety and depression, burdens that would have weighed heavily on a young wife whose public appearance was a matter of family honour.At 24 in 1503, her age is consistent with the early onset typical of extensive alopecia areata. The Telegraph says the condition affects an estimated 400,000 people in the United Kingdom, women more often than men, with symptoms most often starting between the ages of 25 and 29.What the Mona Lisa alopecia study cannot prove, the limits of diagnosing a paintingFew Mona Lisa theories have been settled, and Dr Michael Yafi, who told the European Congress on Obesity in Istanbul that her portrait showed excess body fat, called the many diagnoses fun and interesting. Dr Laino's paper is just as candid about its own limits. It acknowledges the usual caveats of diagnosing the past, assumes the relevant passages are Leonardo's own and well preserved, which the technical evidence supports but cannot place beyond doubt, and cannot rule out a cause that is no longer visible on the panel.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2020, five rainstorms damaged a Georgia solar project; insurer later tried to apply a $2.5 million deductible after paying $600,000
articles.summary: Five heavy rainstorms damaged a solar power project in Georgia between December 2019 and April 2020, leading to an insurance dispute over how the losses
articles.body: Five heavy rainstorms damaged a solar power project in Georgia between December 2019 and April 2020, leading to an insurance dispute over how the losses should be classified. Zurich American Insurance Company initially treated the damage as water-related and made payments totalling $600,000 to First Solar Electric LLC. The insurer later argued that the incidents should be classified as flooding, which carried a much higher deductible of $2.5 million per event. In an October 2026 ruling, a federal appeals court examined whether the insurer could change its position after making the earlier payments.Why did the Georgia solar project face a $2.5 million deductibleThe dispute concerned a large solar power plant that First Solar was constructing in central Georgia. According to the US Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit in its October 2026 opinion, the project covered 1,038 acres and was insured under a master builders risk policy purchased from Zurich American Insurance Company.The policy covered physical damage to the insured property during the construction period. Its coverage ran from 24 August 2017 to 24 August 2020, placing all five rain-related incidents within the insured period.The storms occurred on or around 13 December 2019, 5 February 2020, 13 February 2020, 3 March 2020 and 18 April 2020. As the court explained in its judgment, rainwater accumulated on the ground and spread across the site, damaging solar arrays, access roads, security fences and other construction work, including electrical and structural components.InsuranceJournal reported that the facility was a 200-megawatt solar plant. The damage triggered claims under a policy that treated water damage and flood damage differently, making the classification of each incident central to the dispute.The policy made a distinction between water damage and floodingThe insurance contract set two substantially different deductibles, depending on how the damage was classified. A deductible is the amount that must be accounted for by the insured before the insurer pays for a covered loss.Under the policy, water damage carried a deductible of $100,000 for each event. Flood damage, however, attracted a deductible of $2.5 million per event. The difference meant that the classification could determine whether First Solar received an insurance payment.The Eleventh Circuit's opinion explained that the policy's definition of flooding included the unusual and rapid accumulation or runoff of surface water that temporarily inundated normally dry land. Water damage covered damage caused by water from any source, except damage falling under the policy's flood definition or resulting from a named storm.These provisions became important when Zurich reconsidered its initial assessment. Although the insurer eventually concluded that the incidents qualified as flooding, the court had to determine whether the company could apply the higher deductible after already making payments under its earlier decision.How did Zurich change its position after paying $600,000Zurich assigned adjuster Scott Klaben to investigate First Solar's claims. According to the court's account, Klaben inspected the project in February 2020 and initially recorded the losses as water damage.The insurer subsequently issued three advance payments of $200,000 each for the first three rain events. Together, these payments amounted to $600,000.The court noted that Zurich had not reserved its right to change its coverage decision before making those payments. In other words, the company did not state that it might later reconsider the classification and apply a different deductible.Zurich subsequently reversed its position, treating the losses as flood damage instead of water damage. Because the deductible for flooding was $2.5 million per event, the insurer concluded that the claimed losses did not exceed the applicable deductible and that no further payment was due. It then closed the claim.Insurance Journal reported that this change led to litigation, with First Solar challenging the insurer's attempt to apply the higher deductible after the initial payments.The appeals court examined whether the insurer could reverse its decisionFirst Solar brought the dispute before the US District Court for the Middle District of Georgia. The district court ruled that the flood deductible applied under the policy but that Zurich had waived its right to impose it on the rain-related claims. It also rejected the insurer's argument concerning the timing of the lawsuit.The case proceeded to a trial focused on damages, and a jury found in favour of First Solar. The district court subsequently awarded the company $12.2 million, including interest calculated before the judgment.Both parties appealed aspects of the decision.In its 22 October 2026 opinion, the Eleventh Circuit considered whether Georgia law allowed Zurich to apply the higher deductible after making unconditional payments based on its earlier coverage determination.The court concluded that Zurich had waived its right to apply the flood deductible to the first three incidents. Its reasoning focused on the insurer's initial decision and its failure to reserve the right to change that decision before issuing the payments.As reported by Insurance Journal, the appeals court found that Zurich could not simply reverse its earlier position and impose the higher deductible on those three claims.The ruling leaves two rain events open for further proceedingsThe appeals court did not resolve every aspect of the dispute in First Solar's favour. Its judgment distinguished between the first three rain events and the two later incidents, which occurred on 3 March and 18 April 2020.For the first three events, the court upheld the conclusion that Zurich had waived its right to apply the flood deductible. However, it found that a genuine dispute remained over whether the insurer had also waived that right for the final two incidents.The Eleventh Circuit therefore vacated the judgment concerning the March and April events and sent that part of the case back to the district court for further proceedings. The court also upheld the denial of Zurich's request to strike one of First Solar's witnesses as a sanction.Zurich cannot apply the higher flood deductible to the first three rain events after waiving that right through its earlier actions, while the claims involving the final two incidents require further consideration by the lower court.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran blames US for deal failure, urges new try amid fear of new attacks
articles.summary: Tehran warns that even limited strikes would trigger a response ‘several times greater’.
articles.body:
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has blamed Washington for the unravelling of an interim deal aimed at ending the war with the United States and Israel, amid growing fears that the fighting could resume imminently.

In comments broadcast by Iranian Press TV on Saturday, But Pezeshkian also said that both sides should return to the deal and “conclude it”.

His remarks come amid growing fears that military action could resume as soon as this weekend, after US President Donald Trump said on Friday that he “may do another little Epic Fury”, using the codename of the US-Israeli war against Iran that started on February 28.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has warned that even limited strikes would trigger a response “several times greater”, according to comments reported by the semi-official Fars News Agency.

Iranian Armed Forces Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi said on Saturday that the US military would not be allowed in the Gulf “under any circumstances and at any time”. Abdollahi said Trump could only “dream” of seeing US forces enter the Gulf, adding that he would take his dream to the grave.

Trump has suggested he could take further military action against Iran, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he remains committed to overthrowing the country’s government.

Both leaders face elections, with Israelis set to choose their next government on Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trump’s Republican Party faces crucial midterm elections on November 3, with Democrats potentially winning control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. Such an outcome would be a major blow to Trump, who still has more than two years left in his final term in the White House.

Iranian government spokesperson Fatemeh Mohajerani said on Saturday that Tehran would not “wait for permission to defend itself”, adding that the country “seeks peace but will respond to any aggression with severe consequences”.

“Our position is clear: we do not flee from dialogue for peace, and we do not hesitate in defending the country. Those who harbour the illusion of destroying Iran must correct their calculations,” Mohajerani wrote in a memo.

Her comments came as Iranian judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. The pair discussed how to tackle corruption and pursue compensation for Iranians affected by the US-Israeli war, among other issues.

Khamenei replaced his father as supreme leader after the latter was assassinated during the opening strikes of the war on February 28. He has not been seen in public since assuming the position in early March.

Parliament Speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf was reported to have met Khamenei earlier this week.

articles.title: Democratic senator accused of 'political malpractice' after job ad ignites firestorm over DEI language
articles.summary: The Atlantic dissects Edward Markey's intern job posting encouraging BIPOC and LGBTQ+ applicants that sparked accusations of discrimination against White men.
articles.body: A Democratic senator’s internship job posting was deemed "political malpractice" by an essay in The Atlantic on Friday that argued diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) language can fuel the White identity politics that Democrats oppose. The commentary by Conor Friedersdorf, headlined "The DEI Language That’s Doing More Harm Than Good," pointed to a social media post from Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., in which he sought interns for his Boston office. In the post, Markey wrote, "BIPOC, LGBTQ+, working class, veterans, and other underrepresented candidates with Massachusetts ties are encouraged to apply." TRUMP ADMIN'S PUSH TO SCRAP DEI IN FEDERAL GOVERNMENT TAKES LANDMARK STEP WITH NEW HIRING RULE The senator’s call for applications sparked criticism online, with critics suggesting Markey was openly discriminating against White men while attempting to appear inclusive. The Atlantic essay noted that Manhattan Institute senior fellow Christopher Rufo alleged Markey’s internship posting was an open violation of civil rights law and called on the Justice Department to pursue federal charges. Former Trump Justice Department appointee Theo Wold also weighed in, writing that the goal of the Democratic Party is to make sure White men "have no opportunities to find gainful employment." Friedersdorf called the senator’s wording "political malpractice," arguing that language that fuels White identity politics is harmful to Americans of all races, even when the intent is good. He added that Democrats should instead adopt rhetoric that clearly commits to equal opportunity. "White identitarians would exist even in a world without bias of any sort in recruitment or hiring –– but using language that fuels White identity politics, as Markey’s language did, is political malpractice that’s bad for Americans of all races, no matter how well intentioned it might be," the author wrote. Fox News Digital reached out to Markey's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response. NEW YORK TIMES SUED BY FEDERAL GOVERNMENT OVER ALLEGED 'DEI-RELATED' EMPLOYMENT DISCRIMINATION The article went on to argue that Democrats were more likely than Republicans to support policies that promote diversity in employment opportunities, which Friedersdorf said have prompted credible allegations of discrimination from White men. Friedersdorf added that members of Generation Z are even more likely to perceive discrimination against young, White men, and that generational differences can further exacerbate the sentiment. According to the article, in 2019, about a third of young men said men face some discrimination in America. By 2025, that figure was reportedly 51%. AOC SAYS ‘WOKE 1 WAS CRAZY,’ BUT DEMOCRATS STILL OWE VOTERS AN EXPLANATION However, Markey’s call for applications — and the outrage it sparked — drew the attention of Democratic political strategist Kaivan Shroff, who told Fox News Digital the post may have done more harm than good when it comes to Democrats’ public pledge for equality. "Markey’s post is exactly the kind of virtue signaling that feeds the outrage cycle without actually doing much for diversity," Shroff said. "If your office genuinely wants a broader applicant pool, you should already have relationships with colleges, community groups and organizations that can get the posting in front of those candidates." Shroff added that the senator's post appeared to be more about "announcing your values than doing the harder work of diverse recruiting." "So there is also a basic competence question here," Shroff told Fox News Digital. "A Senate office should not need social media language that makes half the country wonder whether they are less welcome in order to find diverse applicants. That also makes the post look like a substitute for the infrastructure you should already have." The essay concluded by pointing to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., as a model. Her office’s intern job posting describes it as an equal-opportunity employer and encourages "all individuals from all backgrounds" to apply — a notable difference from Markey’s own solicitation. Warren’s approach was echoed by Shroff, who noted how Democrats have increasingly turned social flashpoints into easy lay-ups for their opponents. "The larger political mistake is that Democrats keep handing the right these easy cultural fights for almost no substantive benefit," the Democratic strategist said. "Most people understand the argument for widening opportunity and even rebalancing past unfairness where possible." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "What they resent is language that makes it sound like to lift up one group or groups you have to put down or exclude another and that is just unproductive — and incorrect," Shroff added. "Politics is all about addition and not subtraction, so it’s a wrongheaded approach."
